newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ILO finds SAfrican job rate better than believed.
newsitem.headline: ILO finds SAfrican job rate better than believed.

text.p: The International Labour Organisation (ILO), disputing assertions that South Africa has one of the world's highest unemployment rates, said on Monday many more people there held jobs than official figures showed.

And in a wide-ranging survey commissioned by the South African government, economists from the United Nations agency urged Pretoria to focus as much on combatting poverty and inequality as on job creation.

"The real unemployment figure is probably closer to around 20 percent than the 32 percent typically cited by politicians, economists and the media," chief coordinator of the survey Guy Standing told a news conference.

He said over-estimations of the jobless figures "could fuel labour market interventions that focus largely or exclusively on reducing unemployment at the risk of worsening the problems of poverty and income inequality."

An unemployment figure of between 32-35 per cent is often cited as a potential source of major social unrest to come and one of the main deterrents to the foreign investment the South African government says the country badly needs.

President Nelson Mandela, who has been sending his ministers around the globe to promote the country's attractions for outside capital, is himself heading for South-East Asia this week to seek new investment sources.

The 500-page ILO survey, "Restructuring the Labour Market: The South African Challenge", said official statistics gathered just before and soon after the end of apartheid in 1994 failed to reflect the true employment picture.

Among the reasons were a "pervasive distrust factor" among South African blacks which led them to mislead census-takers, a neglect of mining hostels and small-scale informal activities, and poor coverage of immigrant workers and rural women.

While a 20 percent jobless figure was still serious, the report argued, "it is only one dimension of the labour market crisis facing the country." Poverty and inequality had to be addressed "with at least as much force as unemployment."
But it was also vital to develop efficient mechanisms for improving industrial relations including consultations between employers, labour and the government.

Poverty, it said, had many causes other than unemployment and many of the poorest people actually held jobs. "Sensible redistribution is the key to overcoming the political, social and economic legacy of apartheid," Standing declared.
The ILO economists said inequality of the type found in South Africa -- whose income distribution was "among the most unequal in the world" -- was a major barrier to economic growth.

By international standards, the earnings level of senior managers was very high, and wage differentials had been much greater than in the dynamic emerging economies of South-East Asia and in industrially-developed countries.

The wealthiest South Africans continued to be white urban dwellers and the poorest were black, rural dwellers. Inter- racial inequalities had stabilised in recent years but the gap within racial groups was widening.

The survey urged Pretoria to aim at ensuring a wider share of employment through encouraging shiftwork -- currently far below the levels in the South-East Asian economies. Most South African firms operated only one shift, it said.

"Shiftworking is a way of improving the utilisation of capital equipment and of generating employment, as well as a means of raising total productivity," it said. Low productivity is also often cited as a major deterrent to foreign investment.
